intro: The first five books of the Bible are called the Torah in Jewish tradition and the Pentateuch, "five scrolls," in Greek. They open with creation and close with Moses looking at a land he will not enter. In between are stories of a flood, a family, an escape, and a mountain, and hundreds of laws about worship, food, courts and neighbors. Jews, Christians and Muslims all know these stories, and each tradition reads them in its own way.

In this unit you will read the Torah as literature and as history. As literature, you will watch how the writers build a scene, repeat a pattern, pun on a name, and leave a question open. As history, you will set the text beside what archaeologists have dug up: a flood tablet from Nineveh, a law stone from Babylon, an Egyptian stele that names Israel. You will learn what those finds can say and what they cannot.

By the end you will be able to tell the two creation accounts apart, compare Noah's flood with the Epic of Gilgamesh, follow the promise from Abraham to Joseph, count the Ten Commandments three ways, and explain how Jewish and Christian readers, and modern scholars, read the same page differently. You will report what the text says and who reads it how, without deciding for anyone what to believe.
bigQuestion: How do the five books of the Torah tell a people's story of beginnings, promise and law, and how have different readers understood the same words?

words.d: the first five books of the Bible; Hebrew for "teaching" or "instruction"
the Greek name for the same five books, meaning "five scrolls"
a binding agreement; in the Torah, the bond the text describes between God and Noah, Abraham and Israel
the voice that tells a story; the Torah's narrator reports and rarely explains
the scholarly view that the Torah combines several earlier written sources
a Mesopotamian poem whose eleventh tablet tells a flood story like Noah's
a story that explains how something came to be, such as many languages
Passover, the spring festival that Exodus 12 sets to remember the escape from Egypt
the ten statements of Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5, numbered differently by different traditions
a law in the form "if this happens, then this follows," common in Exodus 21 to 23 and in Hammurabi's laws

test.q: Which name for God does Genesis 1 use?
test.why: Genesis 1 uses Elohim. Genesis 2 and 3 switch to "the LORD God," one of the differences readers notice between the accounts.

test.q: What do traditional readers and source critics share when they read Genesis 1 and 2?
choices: The same text with its differences in order and style
The same explanation for the differences
The belief that chapter 2 is later
The view that Moses wrote both
test.why: Both start from the same two chapters. They differ on how to explain the differences: one story told twice, or two sources joined.

test.q: Which detail appears in the Gilgamesh flood but not in Genesis?
choices: Birds sent out to test the water
Gods gathering like flies around a sacrifice
test.why: Tablet XI describes the gods crowding around Utnapishtim's sacrifice. Genesis has one God who promises never to flood the earth again.

test.q: What sign does Genesis 9 give for the covenant with Noah?
test.why: Genesis 9:13 sets the rainbow as the sign. Circumcision is the sign of the covenant with Abraham in Genesis 17.

test.q: Who is the only person in Genesis to give God a name?
test.why: Genesis 16:13 says Hagar named the God who found her by the spring.

test.q: What does Genesis 32 say the name Israel means?
test.why: After wrestling all night, Jacob is named Israel, which the text explains as striving with God and with people.

test.q: What can archaeology say about Abraham, Isaac and Jacob?
choices: It has found their tombs and names
It has shown they never lived
It describes their world but cannot confirm or deny them
It proves they lived in Egypt
test.why: No inscription names the ancestors. Archaeology fills in the Middle Bronze Age setting; historians say the stories cannot be verified either way.

test.q: What does Pharaoh's daughter do in Exodus 2?
choices: Finds Moses in a basket and raises him
test.why: Exodus 2:5-10 says Pharaoh's daughter found the basket, took pity, and named the child Moses.

test.q: How does the King James Version translate God's answer at the burning bush?
test.why: Exodus 3:14 in the KJV reads "I AM THAT I AM." The 1917 JPS leaves the Hebrew untranslated.
Exodus 12 gives the instructions for the lamb, the unleavened bread and the yearly remembrance that is Passover, Pesach.

test.q: In the Protestant and Orthodox count, what is the second commandment?
choices: Thou shalt not make a graven image
I am the LORD thy God
test.why: Reformed Protestants and Orthodox Christians count "no other gods" first and "no graven image" second. Jews and Catholics join them into one.

test.q: Which two law collections both contain a law about a goring ox?
choices: The Covenant Code in Exodus and Hammurabi's laws
test.why: Exodus 21 and Hammurabi's laws, about 1750 BCE, both rule on an ox that gores, one of the closest parallels between them.

test.q: Where does "love thy neighbour as thyself" first appear?
test.why: Leviticus 19:18 is the source. Mark 12 quotes it alongside Deuteronomy 6:5.

test.q: What does the Merneptah Stele show about Israel?
choices: That a people called Israel lived in Canaan by about 1208 BCE
test.why: The stele lists Israel among peoples in Canaan. It says nothing about an escape from Egypt.

test.q: Which describes the Deuteronomy 6:4 translation difference correctly?
choices: KJV and JPS 1917 supply the verb "is" in different places
test.why: The Hebrew has no verb. KJV reads "The LORD our God is one LORD"; JPS 1917 reads "the LORD our God, the LORD is one."

write.prompt: How does the Torah use a story to explain a law? Choose one law and one story, for example Exodus 20:2 and the escape from Egypt, Leviticus 19:34 and Genesis 12, or Deuteronomy 5:15 and Exodus 1. Cite two or three passages by book, chapter and verse. Explain what each says, how the story and the law connect, and how at least two different readers, Jewish, Christian or scholarly, have read them.
tips: Name every passage you use: book, chapter and verse, and the translation.
Attribute each reading: "Jewish tradition reads," "many scholars think," "Christian readers often."
Compare readings; do not rank them or say which is true.
Use the unit's terms: covenant, case law, narrator, etiology, Shema.
Start from what the text says, then move to what it has meant.

title: The Pentateuch as Literature and History

chapters.title: Genesis: Creation, Flood, Ancestors
chapters.bigQuestion: How does Genesis tell the story of beginnings, and what do its readers, ancient and modern, make of it?

story.title: The Tablet in the Glass Case
story.kicker: A broken piece of clay tells of a flood and a boat, and it is older than any copy of Genesis.
paragraphs: In 1872 a young man named George Smith sat at a table in the British Museum in London. He was sorting broken clay tablets dug up in the ruins of Nineveh, in what is now Iraq. The tablets were covered in tiny wedge-shaped marks called cuneiform. Smith had taught himself to read them. That day he picked up a piece and began to read a story he thought he knew.

The tablet told of a great flood sent by the gods. One man was warned. He built a huge boat, loaded it with his family and animals, and rode out the storm. When the rain stopped, the boat came to rest on a mountain. The man sent out birds to see if the water had gone down. Smith was so excited that, the story goes, he jumped up and began to undress in the middle of the museum.

The tablet was part of the Epic of Gilgamesh, a long poem from ancient Mesopotamia. The copy Smith read was made in the 600s BCE for a king's library. Older versions of the flood story go back hundreds of years before that. The oldest surviving copies of Genesis, the Dead Sea Scrolls, were written centuries later than Smith's tablet.

Today you can see flood tablets in museums, including a collection at the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures at the University of Chicago. Students who read Genesis 6 to 9 beside Gilgamesh Tablet XI notice the likenesses right away. They also notice the differences. What those likenesses and differences mean is a question readers have argued about ever since 1872.
story.think: If two ancient stories share a boat, a flood and birds, what are the different ways a reader might explain that?

lessons.title: Seven Days in Genesis 1
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 1 tells creation as an ordered week, with a pattern of speech, making, naming and rest.
reading: The Bible opens with a short, careful passage. Genesis 1:1 to 2:3 tells of creation in six days, followed by a seventh day of rest. Each day follows a pattern. God speaks, something comes to be, God sees that it is good, and evening and morning close the day. The pattern repeats like a refrain in a song. Readers of Hebrew notice that the passage is built from repeated phrases.

The days pair up. On days one to three the text says God makes light, sky and sea, and dry land with plants. On days four to six the text fills those spaces: sun, moon and stars; birds and fish; land animals and people. On day six, the story says, God makes humans "in the image of God," both male and female. On day seven God rests, and the day is made holy.

Jewish tradition connects the seventh day to *Shabbat*, the weekly day of rest. Many Christians connect it to Sunday worship. Scholars who study the Bible as literature point to its shape: a *refrain*, a count of days, and a balance between the first three days and the last three. The first thing a reader can do is simply see that shape.

The Hebrew name for this book is *Bereshit*, its first word, meaning "in the beginning." The English name Genesis comes from a Greek word for origin. Both names point to the same thing. This is a book about how things started, as its writers told it.

words.d: the first book of the Bible; its Hebrew name, Bereshit, means "in the beginning"
a line or phrase repeated again and again in a text, like a chorus in a song
the Jewish Sabbath, a weekly day of rest from Friday evening to Saturday evening

look.title: The First Verse in the King James Version
look.text: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
look.prompt: Read the verse aloud. Which words does the writer choose to start the whole Bible with, and why might that matter?

check.q: Which pattern repeats through the days in Genesis 1?
choices: God speaks, a thing comes to be, God sees it is good, evening and morning
A prophet speaks, a king obeys, a city is built
A man plants, a woman harvests, a feast is held
God sleeps, a storm comes, the earth is flooded
check.why: Genesis 1 is built on a refrain: God speaks, the thing appears, God sees it is good, and evening and morning end the day.

check.q: What happens on the seventh day in Genesis 2:1-3?
choices: God creates the sun and moon
God rests and makes the day holy
check.why: The text says God finished the work, rested on the seventh day, and blessed it. Jewish tradition connects this to Shabbat.

check.q: What does the Hebrew name Bereshit mean?
check.why: Hebrew books are often named for their first word. Bereshit means "in the beginning."

lessons.title: A Garden in Genesis 2
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 2 tells of creation again, in a different order and style, centered on a garden and a first human pair.
reading: Starting at Genesis 2:4, the story begins again. The style changes. There is no count of days. The text says the LORD God forms a man from the dust of the ground and breathes life into him. Then God plants a garden in *Eden* and puts the man there to tend it. Only after that does the text say God makes animals, and last of all a woman from the man's side.

The order is different from Genesis 1. In chapter 1, plants and animals come before people. In chapter 2, the man comes first, then the garden, then the animals, then the woman. God is also drawn differently. In chapter 1 God speaks from a distance. In chapter 2 God forms, plants, walks and talks, more like a potter or a gardener.

Genesis 3 continues the garden story. A talking serpent, a forbidden tree, a choice, and a leaving of the garden. Christian tradition often reads this as "the Fall," the start of human sin. Jewish tradition reads it in many ways, and often does not use that term. The text itself never uses the word sin in chapter 3. Noticing what the text says, and what later readers added, is part of reading closely.

The two names matter too. Genesis 1 calls the creator "God" (Hebrew *Elohim*). Genesis 2 and 3 use "the LORD God," where LORD stands for the four-letter Hebrew name that many Jews do not pronounce. Many English Bibles print LORD in small capitals to mark it.

words.d: the garden in Genesis 2 and 3 where the text places the first humans
the Hebrew word for God used in Genesis 1; Genesis 2 adds the name printed as LORD
a Christian term for the events of Genesis 3, read as the start of human sin; the text itself does not use the term

look.title: Dust and Breath
look.text: And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
look.prompt: Compare this with Genesis 1:27, where God creates by speaking. What picture of God does each verse give?

check.q: In Genesis 2, what is made first?
check.why: Genesis 2:7 tells of the man formed from dust before the garden, the animals and the woman.

check.q: Which name for God appears in Genesis 1 but not in Genesis 2 and 3?
choices: Elohim, translated God, appears alone in chapter 1
The LORD appears alone in chapter 1
check.why: Genesis 1 uses Elohim, "God." Genesis 2 and 3 use "the LORD God," adding the four-letter name.

check.q: Which statement about "the Fall" is accurate?
choices: The word appears in Genesis 3 in Hebrew
It is a Christian term for Genesis 3; Jewish readings often do not use it
It is the Jewish name for Genesis 3
It is the name of the serpent in Genesis 3
check.why: "The Fall" is a Christian reading of Genesis 3. The text does not use the term, and Jewish tradition reads the chapter in many ways.

lessons.title: Two Accounts, Many Readers
lessons.mainIdea: Readers have handled the two creation accounts in different ways: as one story told twice, as two sources joined, or as a general view followed by a close-up.
reading: Put Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 side by side and the differences show. The order of creation is not the same. The name for God is not the same. The style is not the same. Ancient readers noticed this long before modern scholars did. The question is what to do with it.

One old answer says the two chapters are one story told twice. Chapter 1 gives the wide view. Chapter 2 zooms in on the sixth day. Many Jewish and Christian readers today still read it this way. Rabbis in the ancient *Midrash* and Christian writers like Augustine (354 to 430 CE) each offered ways to fit the chapters together.

Another answer, common among scholars since the 1800s, is that the Torah joins older written *sources*. In this view, Genesis 1 comes from one source, often called the Priestly source, and Genesis 2 from another. A later editor placed them side by side. The German scholar Julius Wellhausen made this view famous in 1878. It is called the documentary hypothesis. Many scholars accept a version of it. Others, including many religious readers, do not.
In a public school, the job is not to pick the true reading. It is to know the text, know the readings, and say who holds each one. That is what the study of the Bible as literature means.

words.d: ancient Jewish commentary that explores and fills gaps in the biblical text
in Bible study, an older written text that scholars think an editor used to build a book
the scholarly view, made famous by Julius Wellhausen in 1878, that the Torah combines several earlier written sources

look.title: Side by Side
look.text: Column A, Genesis 1: God (Elohim) speaks; six days; plants, then animals, then humans, male and female together. Column B, Genesis 2: the LORD God forms; no days; the man, then the garden, then the animals, then the woman. Reader 1 says: one story, wide shot then close-up. Reader 2 says: two older texts placed side by side by an editor.
look.prompt: Which details in the columns would each reader point to in support of their view? Can both readers be honest about the same text?

check.q: What does the documentary hypothesis claim?
choices: Moses wrote Genesis on Mount Sinai
The Torah joins several earlier written sources
Genesis 2 was added in the Middle Ages
check.why: The documentary hypothesis, made famous by Wellhausen in 1878, holds that the Torah combines older sources joined by editors.

check.q: How do many traditional readers fit Genesis 1 and 2 together?
choices: They say chapter 2 is a mistake
They read chapter 1 as the wide view and chapter 2 as a close-up of day six
They say chapter 2 describes a second world
check.why: A common traditional reading treats the two chapters as one story: a general account, then a detailed account of the sixth day.

check.q: What is Midrash?
choices: A Greek translation of the Torah
A kind of ancient Jewish commentary on the Bible
The name of the Priestly source
check.why: Midrash is rabbinic commentary that explores and expands the biblical text. It is not a translation or a creed.

lessons.title: Cain and Abel
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 4 tells of the first brothers, the first murder, and a question the text leaves the reader to answer.
reading: Genesis 4 moves fast. Two brothers bring offerings. Cain, a farmer, brings crops. Abel, a shepherd, brings the best of his flock. The text says God accepts Abel's offering but not Cain's. It does not say why. Cain grows angry. God warns him that sin waits "at the door." Then Cain leads his brother into a field and kills him.

The *narrator* of Genesis rarely explains. That is a mark of the book's style. When God asks, "Where is Abel thy brother?" Cain answers with a question of his own: "Am I my brother's keeper?" The text does not answer him. Readers have filled that silence for thousands of years. Jewish Midrash imagined what the brothers argued about. Christian writers read Abel as the first innocent victim.

God punishes Cain with wandering, but also marks him so no one will kill him. Cain builds a city and starts a line of children. Readers notice that the story mixes judgment and protection. It also asks a question the rest of the Bible keeps asking: what do people owe one another?
The phrase "my brother's keeper" has entered everyday English. Speakers use it in speeches about duty to neighbors. Knowing where it comes from helps you hear what a speaker is doing with it.

words.d: the voice that tells a story; the narrator of Genesis reports events and rarely explains them
a gift brought to God; in Genesis 4, Cain brings crops and Abel brings animals from his flock

look.title: A Question Left Open
look.text: And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?
look.prompt: The text never answers Cain's question. What do you think the writer wants the reader to do with it?

check.q: Why does the text say God rejected Cain's offering?
choices: Because Cain was the older brother
The text does not give a reason
check.why: Genesis 4 reports that Cain's offering was not accepted but does not explain why. The narrator's silence is part of the story's style.

check.q: What does the phrase "my brother's keeper" come from?
choices: Cain's reply to God's question in Genesis 4:9
check.why: Cain answers God's question "Where is Abel thy brother?" with "Am I my brother's keeper?" in Genesis 4:9.

check.q: What does God do after judging Cain?
choices: Marks him so no one will kill him
check.why: Genesis 4:15 says God put a mark on Cain to protect him from being killed, mixing judgment with protection.

lessons.title: Noah and the Flood
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 6 to 9 tells of a flood, an ark, and a covenant marked by a rainbow.
reading: Genesis 6 says the earth has filled with violence. God decides to send a flood but tells Noah to build an *ark*, a huge boat. Noah loads his family and animals. Rain falls for forty days and nights. The waters cover the mountains. When they go down, the ark rests on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sends out a raven, then a dove, to test whether the land is dry.

After the flood, Noah builds an altar. God promises never again to destroy the earth by flood. The text calls this a *covenant*, a binding agreement. Its sign is the rainbow. God also gives rules to Noah and his sons: do not eat blood, and do not shed human blood. Jewish tradition later called these and other rules the seven laws of the children of Noah.

Careful readers notice that the flood story seems to say some things twice. Noah is told to bring two of each animal in one place, and seven pairs of clean animals in another. The rain lasts forty days in one verse and the waters rise for 150 days in another. Traditional readers explain these as different stages of one event. Many scholars see two sources woven together. Both readings start from the same text.

The flood story is read every year in synagogues in the Torah reading called Noach. It is retold in the Qur'an, where Noah is the prophet Nuh. It appears in children's books, art and film. Each retelling chooses what to keep.

words.d: the large boat that Genesis 6 says Noah built to survive the flood
a binding agreement; in Genesis 9, God's promise never to flood the earth again, with the rainbow as its sign
the mountains where Genesis 8:4 says the ark came to rest

look.title: Numbers in the Flood Story
look.prompt: Which of these numbers seem to overlap or repeat? How might a traditional reader and a source-critical scholar each explain that?

check.q: What is the sign of the covenant in Genesis 9?
check.why: Genesis 9:13 names the rainbow as the sign of God's promise never to flood the earth again.

check.q: Which birds does Noah send out in Genesis 8?
check.why: Genesis 8:7-12 says Noah sent out a raven, then a dove, to see whether the waters had gone down.

check.q: How do many scholars explain the repeated details in the flood story?
choices: The story was copied badly in the Middle Ages
The text was first written in Greek
Two older sources were woven together
check.why: Source critics see two accounts combined; traditional readers see stages of one event. Both readings begin from the same text.

lessons.title: The Tablet and the Ark
lessons.mainIdea: The Mesopotamian flood story in the Epic of Gilgamesh is like Genesis in many details and different in its meaning.
reading: The *Epic of Gilgamesh* is a long poem from ancient *Mesopotamia*, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Its hero, a king named Gilgamesh, goes looking for a way to live forever. He finds an old man, Utnapishtim, who survived a great flood. On the eleventh tablet of the poem, Utnapishtim tells his story.

The likenesses to Genesis are striking. A god warns one man. The man builds a boat and coats it with pitch. He brings his family and animals aboard. A storm floods the world. The boat lands on a mountain. The man sends out birds: a dove, a swallow and a raven. He offers a sacrifice, and the gods gather around it. Some flood stories from Mesopotamia are older than 1700 BCE, long before the earliest likely dates for Genesis.

The differences matter just as much. In Gilgamesh, the gods send the flood because people are too noisy and too many. In Genesis, the text says God acts because of violence. In Gilgamesh, one god secretly warns the hero against the wishes of the others. In Genesis, one God decides, warns and saves. In Gilgamesh, the survivor becomes immortal. In Genesis, Noah receives a covenant and grows a vineyard.

Scholars debate how the stories are connected. Most think the Genesis writers knew a Mesopotamian flood story and retold it with their own meaning. Some religious readers hold that both stories remember one real event. The public-school reader's task is to see the likeness, name the difference, and report how readers explain them.

words.d: a long ancient Mesopotamian poem about a king who seeks eternal life; its eleventh tablet tells a flood story
the ancient land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, mostly in today's Iraq
wedge-shaped writing pressed into clay, used in Mesopotamia for about 3,000 years

look.title: Two Boats, Two Reasons
look.text: Gilgamesh, Tablet XI: the gods decide on a flood; the god Ea whispers a warning to Utnapishtim through a reed wall; after the flood the gods crowd like flies around his sacrifice. Genesis 6 to 8: God sees the earth filled with violence; God tells Noah to build an ark; after the flood God smells the offering and promises never to flood the earth again.
look.prompt: Pick one detail the stories share and one they do not. What does each difference suggest about how the writers thought about God or the gods?

check.q: Who tells the flood story in the Epic of Gilgamesh?
check.why: On Tablet XI, the flood survivor Utnapishtim tells Gilgamesh how he built the boat and lived through the flood.

check.q: Which reason for the flood belongs to Gilgamesh, not Genesis?
choices: The earth was full of violence
People were too noisy and too many
check.why: Mesopotamian flood stories say the gods were disturbed by human noise and numbers. Genesis 6 speaks of violence.

check.q: What do most scholars think about the link between the two stories?
choices: Genesis retells a Mesopotamian flood story with its own meaning
Both were written by the same author
check.why: Most scholars think the Genesis writers knew a Mesopotamian flood tradition, which is older, and reshaped it. Other readers hold different views.

lessons.title: The Tower of Babel
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 11 explains many languages through a short story about a tower, a name, and a scattering.
reading: Genesis 11:1-9 is only nine verses long. It says all people once spoke one language. They settle on a plain in Shinar, which readers have long linked to *Babylon*. They bake bricks and plan a city with a tower reaching heaven, "to make us a name." God comes down, mixes their language, and scatters them. The city is called *Babel*, a play on the Hebrew word for confusion.

The story works like an *etiology*, a tale that explains how something came to be. Here it explains why people speak many languages and live in many lands. Ancient Mesopotamian cities did build stepped towers called ziggurats, some of them enormous. The writers of Genesis likely knew them. The story turns a proud building into a lesson about limits.

Readers have found different meanings in Babel. Some read it as a judgment on pride. Some read it as a story about the value of many peoples and tongues. Some read it beside Genesis 10, the table of nations, which already lists many languages. The narrator, as usual, does not say what the story means.
The story also uses wordplay. Babel sounds like the Hebrew verb for mixing up. Puns on names appear all through Genesis. Noticing them is one way to read the book as its first hearers might have.

words.d: the city of the tower story in Genesis 11; the name puns on a Hebrew word for confusion
a story that explains how something in the world came to be, such as many languages
a stepped tower built beside temples in Mesopotamian cities

look.title: To Make Us a Name
look.text: And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.
look.prompt: What do the builders say they want? What happens to that wish by the end of verse 9?

check.q: What does the Babel story explain, as an etiology?
choices: Why there are seven days in a week
check.why: Genesis 11:1-9 tells how one language became many and how people scattered across the earth.

check.q: What real Mesopotamian building is the tower most often compared to?
check.why: Mesopotamian cities built stepped temple towers called ziggurats, which the Genesis writers likely knew.

check.q: What does the narrator of Genesis 11 tell us the story means?
choices: That many languages are a gift
check.why: As elsewhere in Genesis, the narrator reports the events and leaves the meaning to readers, who have read it in several ways.

lessons.title: Abraham, Sarah and Hagar
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 12 to 25 tells of a promise to Abraham and Sarah, and of Hagar and Ishmael, whose story the text also honors.
reading: In Genesis 12 the story narrows from all peoples to one family. The text says God tells Abram to leave his home in *Mesopotamia* and go to a land he will be shown. God promises him land, many descendants, and that through him all families of the earth will be blessed. Abram goes. Later God renames him Abraham and his wife Sarai becomes Sarah.

The promise runs into a problem. Sarah has no children. She gives her Egyptian servant *Hagar* to Abraham, and Hagar bears Ishmael. Sarah then treats Hagar harshly, and Hagar runs away. The text says God's messenger finds her by a spring and promises that her son too will become a great nation. Hagar gives God a name of her own, the only person in Genesis to do so.

Sarah bears Isaac in old age. Ishmael and Hagar are sent away, and again the text says God hears them. Genesis 17 tells of *circumcision* as the sign of the covenant with Abraham. In Genesis 22, God tests Abraham by asking for Isaac; a ram is offered in his place. Jewish tradition calls this the Akedah, the binding of Isaac. Christian readers have often linked it to Jesus. Muslims recall a similar test, and many hold that the son was Ishmael.

Three traditions look back to Abraham: Judaism, Christianity and Islam. For that reason people sometimes call them the Abrahamic faiths. Each reads his story in its own way. The text itself gives the promise to Isaac's line and also blesses Ishmael's.

words.d: Sarah's Egyptian servant in Genesis 16 and 21, mother of Ishmael
removal of the foreskin; Genesis 17 makes it the sign of the covenant with Abraham
the Hebrew name for the binding of Isaac in Genesis 22
a common name for Judaism, Christianity and Islam, which all look back to Abraham

look.title: The Promise
look.text: And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing.
look.prompt: Compare this with Genesis 11:4, where the builders want to "make us a name." What is the writer doing by placing the two so close together?

check.q: Which three things does the text say God promises Abram in Genesis 12?
choices: Gold, a palace and a crown
A city, a tower and a name
Land, descendants and blessing for all families
A boat, a rainbow and a vineyard
check.why: Genesis 12:1-3 promises land, a great nation, and blessing that reaches all the families of the earth.

check.q: Who is Hagar?
choices: Sarah's Egyptian servant and Ishmael's mother
check.why: Genesis 16 introduces Hagar as Sarah's Egyptian servant, who bears Ishmael.

check.q: What is the Akedah?
choices: The binding of Isaac in Genesis 22
check.why: Akedah is the Hebrew term for the binding of Isaac, when Genesis 22 says Abraham was tested.

lessons.title: Isaac, Rebekah and Jacob
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 24 to 36 follows the promise through Rebekah's cleverness, Jacob's trickery, and a night wrestling that gives Israel its name.
reading: Genesis 24 is the longest chapter in the book. A servant travels back to Abraham's homeland to find a wife for Isaac. He meets *Rebekah* at a well, where she waters his camels. She agrees to go. Wells are meeting places all through Genesis. Readers learn to expect a marriage when a stranger stops at one.

Rebekah bears twins, Esau and *Jacob*. The text says God tells her the older will serve the younger. Esau is a hunter, his father's favorite. Jacob is quiet, his mother's favorite. Jacob buys Esau's birthright for a bowl of stew. Then, with Rebekah's plan, he tricks the blind Isaac into giving him Esau's blessing. Jacob flees to his uncle Laban.

In Laban's house, Jacob the trickster is tricked. He works seven years for Rachel and wakes married to her sister Leah. He works seven more. Between them, and their servants Bilhah and Zilpah, twelve sons and a daughter are born. Coming home, Jacob wrestles all night with a stranger at the river Jabbok. He is given a new name, *Israel*. Genesis 32 says the name means one who struggles with God.

Jacob is not a simple hero. The narrator shows his lies and his limps. Jewish tradition has both praised and questioned him. What the text makes clear is that the promise passes through people who are far from perfect.

words.d: Isaac's wife, who meets his servant at a well in Genesis 24 and later helps Jacob win the blessing
Rebekah's younger twin, who gains Esau's birthright and blessing and is renamed Israel
the extra share and leading place that belonged to a firstborn son
the name Genesis 32 gives Jacob after the night wrestling; later the name of his descendants

look.title: The Trickster Tricked
look.text: Scene 1, Genesis 27: Jacob puts on goatskins so his blind father will think he is hairy Esau, and takes the blessing. Scene 2, Genesis 29: Laban brings Leah to Jacob in the dark, veiled, and Jacob wakes beside the wrong sister. Laban says: in our place the younger is not given before the firstborn.
look.prompt: The narrator never says Jacob got what he deserved. How does the writer hint at it anyway? Find the echo between the two scenes.

check.q: Where does Abraham's servant meet Rebekah?
check.why: Genesis 24 sets the meeting at a well, a place where several Genesis marriages begin.

check.q: What does Jacob trade for Esau's birthright?
check.why: Genesis 25 says Esau, hungry from the field, sold his birthright to Jacob for bread and stew.

check.q: What does Genesis 32 say the name Israel means?
check.why: After the night wrestling, Jacob is named Israel, which the text explains as striving with God and with people.

lessons.title: Joseph in Egypt
lessons.mainIdea: The Joseph story, Genesis 37 to 50, is a long, shaped tale that carries the family into Egypt and sets up the book of Exodus.
reading: Jacob loves *Joseph* more than his other sons and gives him a fine coat. Joseph tells his brothers about dreams in which they bow to him. They sell him to traders bound for Egypt. They dip the coat in goat's blood and tell their father a wild animal killed him. Readers notice the goat and the coat: Jacob, who fooled his father with goatskins, is fooled by his sons.

In Egypt, Joseph rises, falls, and rises again. He is jailed on a false charge. In prison he interprets dreams. When Pharaoh dreams of seven fat cows and seven thin ones, Joseph is called. He explains seven years of plenty and seven of famine, and Pharaoh puts him in charge. When famine comes, Joseph's brothers arrive to buy grain. They do not know him.

Joseph tests his brothers before he reveals himself. The scene where he weeps and says "I am Joseph" is one of the most famous in the Bible. Jacob and the whole family move to Egypt. Near the end, Joseph tells his brothers that what they meant for harm, God meant for good. The book ends with Joseph's death in Egypt and his wish to be buried in Canaan.

Unlike the Abraham stories, the Joseph story is one long, tightly built narrative. Scholars call it a *novella*. Its dreams come in pairs, its scenes echo one another, and God never speaks directly in it. Later readers made it into plays, paintings and a Broadway musical.

words.d: Jacob's favored son, sold into Egypt by his brothers, who rises to rule under Pharaoh
the title of the king of Egypt
a short novel; scholars use the word for the tightly built Joseph story

look.title: Meant for Good
look.text: But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
look.prompt: God never speaks in the Joseph story. How does this line, spoken by Joseph, tell the reader how to understand everything before it?

check.q: How is Jacob tricked by his sons?
choices: They hide Joseph in a well
They show him Joseph's coat dipped in goat's blood
They tell him Joseph became Pharaoh
check.why: Genesis 37 says the brothers dipped Joseph's coat in goat's blood, echoing Jacob's own goatskin trick in Genesis 27.

check.q: What does Joseph explain to Pharaoh?
choices: Seven years of plenty, then seven of famine
The meaning of the name Israel
check.why: In Genesis 41, Joseph reads Pharaoh's dreams as seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine.

check.q: Why do scholars call the Joseph story a novella?
choices: Because it was written in Italian
Because it is one long, tightly built narrative
Because God speaks in every scene
check.why: Genesis 37 to 50 is a single shaped story with paired dreams and echoing scenes, unlike the shorter Abraham episodes.

lessons.title: What the Spade Can Say
lessons.mainIdea: Archaeology can describe the world the ancestor stories are set in, but it cannot confirm or deny the people themselves.
reading: Genesis gives no dates for Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Adding up the Bible's own numbers, traditional readers place them around 2000 to 1700 BCE, in the Middle Bronze Age. *Archaeology* has found a great deal about that world: cities, trade routes, camel bones, tablets with names like those in Genesis, and laws about marriage and servants.

What archaeology has not found is the ancestors themselves. No inscription names Abraham or Jacob. That is not surprising. Herding families rarely left written records. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, but it is also not evidence. Historians say the ancestor stories cannot be checked the way a king's reign can.

Scholars disagree about how to use the stories. Some point to details, like customs known from Mesopotamian tablets at Nuzi and Mari, as signs of old memory. Others note that camels, Philistines and Arameans in the stories fit better with the first millennium BCE, when they think the stories were written down. Religious readers may hold that the stories are true whatever the spade finds.

In a public-school class, the fair statement is this: archaeology can show what the world of Genesis looked like, and it cannot prove or disprove the family stories. Both religious and non-religious readers can agree on that much.

words.d: the study of the past through things people left behind, such as buildings, tools and writing
roughly 2000 to 1550 BCE in the ancient Near East, the period traditional readers assign to the ancestors
words carved or written on stone, clay or another lasting surface

look.title: How Long Is Genesis?
look.cite: Chapter counts of the five books of the Torah, standard in Hebrew and English Bibles
look.prompt: Genesis 1 to 11 covers all peoples; Genesis 12 to 50 covers one family. Roughly what share of the book is about the ancestors?

check.q: What has archaeology found about Abraham himself?
choices: His tomb at Hebron with an inscription
check.why: No ancient inscription names Abraham, Isaac or Jacob. Archaeology describes their world, not the people.

check.q: Which period do traditional readers assign to the ancestors, using the Bible's numbers?
choices: c. 2000-1700 BCE, the Middle Bronze Age
c. 1000 BCE, the time of David
check.why: Adding the Bible's own figures places the ancestors around 2000 to 1700 BCE, within the Middle Bronze Age.

check.q: What is a fair statement about archaeology and the ancestor stories?
choices: Archaeology shows they were written in Egypt
Archaeology describes their world but cannot confirm or deny the people
check.why: The stories cannot be checked the way a king's reign can. Archaeology fills in the setting, not the family.

review.q: Which detail belongs to Genesis 1 and not Genesis 2?
choices: A woman made from the man's side
review.why: Genesis 1 is built on a six-day count. The garden, the woman from the man's side and the serpent belong to chapters 2 and 3.

review.q: Who read the Gilgamesh flood tablet at the British Museum in 1872?
review.why: George Smith, a self-taught reader of cuneiform, recognized the flood story on a tablet from Nineveh in 1872.

review.q: In Gilgamesh, how does the hero learn of the coming flood?
choices: All the gods tell him together
review.why: In Tablet XI the god Ea warns Utnapishtim through a reed wall, against the plan of the other gods. Genesis has one God warn Noah openly.

review.q: What is a covenant, as Genesis uses the word?
choices: A binding agreement between God and people
review.why: Covenant means a binding agreement. Genesis 9 and 17 use it for God's promises to Noah and to Abraham.

review.q: Which person in Genesis gives God a name of her own?
review.why: Genesis 16:13 says Hagar named the God who spoke to her, the only person in Genesis to do so.

review.q: What does the documentary hypothesis say about Genesis 1 and 2?
choices: Both came from the same night vision
They come from different written sources joined by an editor
review.why: The hypothesis holds that the two accounts come from different sources, later combined. Many traditional readers read them as one story instead.

review.q: How does the Joseph story end the book of Genesis?
choices: With the family settled in Egypt and Joseph's death
With the crossing of the sea
With Jacob wrestling at the Jabbok
review.why: Genesis 50 ends with Jacob's family in Egypt and Joseph's death, which sets up the book of Exodus.

review.q: Which is the most careful way to state what archaeology says about the ancestors?
choices: It proves the stories happened as written
It shows the stories are false
It cannot be applied to the Bible
It describes their world but cannot confirm or deny the people
review.why: Archaeology fills in the Middle Bronze Age setting. No inscription names the ancestors, and historians say the stories cannot be verified either way.

chapters.title: Exodus to Deuteronomy: Covenant and Law
chapters.bigQuestion: How do Exodus through Deuteronomy turn a story of escape into a set of laws, and how have readers counted, kept and debated those laws?

story.title: At the Foot of the Mountain
story.kicker: A people camps below a mountain, and the story says a list of ten things is carved in stone.
paragraphs: Exodus 19 sets the scene. Three months after leaving Egypt, the text says, the people of Israel camp in a desert below a mountain called Sinai. Moses climbs up. He comes down with a message: if the people keep God's covenant, they will be a treasured people. The people answer together that they will do all that has been said. Then they are told to wash, wait, and keep off the mountain.

On the third day, the story says, there is thunder, lightning, a thick cloud and a trumpet sound growing louder. The mountain smokes. The people tremble. Then, in Exodus 20, a voice speaks ten things. Jewish tradition calls them the Ten Words. English speakers call them the Ten Commandments. The text says they were later written on two tablets of stone.

The people, the text says, cannot bear to hear more. They ask Moses to listen for them. He goes up into the cloud and stays forty days. Below, the people grow restless and make a golden calf. Moses comes down, sees it, and smashes the tablets. Later he climbs again and returns with a second set. The story does not hide how quickly a promise can break.

Ever since, readers have counted those ten things. Jews count them one way. Catholics and Lutherans count another. Most other Protestants and Orthodox Christians count a third way. All of them read the same verses. In this chapter you will read Exodus 20 in two translations and count for yourself. Then you will follow the laws through Leviticus and Deuteronomy, and ask what historians can say about Egypt, the desert and the mountain.
story.think: Why might a story put a list of laws right after a scene of thunder, smoke and fear? What does the setting do to the list?

lessons.title: Slavery and a Basket
lessons.mainIdea: Exodus opens with Jacob's family grown into a people, enslaved in Egypt, and a baby saved by women who defy Pharaoh.
reading: The book of *Exodus* begins where Genesis ended, in Egypt. Its Hebrew name is *Shemot*, "names," from its first verse, which lists the sons of Jacob. Generations pass. The family becomes a people. A new *Pharaoh*, the text says, does not remember Joseph. He fears the Israelites and forces them to build his store cities with brick and mortar.

Pharaoh then orders that Hebrew baby boys be killed. The story turns on women who refuse. Two midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, disobey and are rewarded. A mother hides her baby in a basket among the reeds of the Nile. His sister watches. Pharaoh's own daughter finds him, takes pity, and raises him as her son. She names him *Moses*.

Moses grows up in the palace but knows his people. When he sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, he kills the Egyptian and flees to Midian. There he marries and tends sheep. The text says that years later God hears the groaning of the enslaved people and remembers the covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Readers have long noticed that the story's first heroes are women: midwives, a mother, a sister, a princess. Jewish tradition praises the midwives by name. The Exodus story has also spoken to enslaved and oppressed people far from Egypt, including African Americans who sang of Moses and the river in spirituals.

words.d: the second book of the Bible, telling of Israel's escape from Egypt; the Greek name means "going out"
the Hebrew name of Exodus, meaning "names," from its first verse
the Hebrew child raised in Pharaoh's palace who, the text says, leads Israel out of Egypt
the title of the king of Egypt; Exodus never gives the king's personal name

look.title: Who Saves the Baby?
look.text: Exodus 1 and 2 name Shiphrah and Puah, the midwives who refuse Pharaoh's order. They do not name the baby's mother or sister, or Pharaoh's daughter, though later texts do. Pharaoh himself is never named in the whole book. The most powerful man in the story has no name; two midwives do.
look.prompt: What might the writer be saying by naming the midwives and not the king? How does that choice shape who the reader remembers?

check.q: What does the Hebrew name Shemot mean?
check.why: Hebrew books are named for opening words. Shemot, "names," comes from the list of Jacob's sons in Exodus 1:1.

check.q: Who disobeys Pharaoh's order to kill Hebrew boys?
check.why: Exodus 1:15-21 names the midwives Shiphrah and Puah, who refuse the order and are rewarded.

check.q: Who raises Moses in the palace?
check.why: Exodus 2 says Pharaoh's daughter found the basket, took pity, and raised the child as her son.

lessons.title: The Burning Bush
lessons.mainIdea: At a bush that burns without burning up, the text says God gives Moses a task and a name.
reading: Exodus 3 finds Moses tending his father-in-law's sheep near a mountain called Horeb, which the text also calls the mountain of God. He sees a bush on fire that does not burn up. He turns aside to look. A voice tells him to take off his shoes, because the ground is holy. The voice names itself as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

Moses is given a job: go to Pharaoh and bring the people out. He objects five times. Who am I? What is your name? What if they do not believe me? I am slow of speech. Send someone else. The text gives an answer to each, including a helper, his brother *Aaron*, who will speak for him.

The most discussed answer is to the question about the name. In Hebrew the reply is *Ehyeh asher ehyeh*. The King James Version renders it "I AM THAT I AM." The 1917 Jewish Publication Society Tanakh leaves the Hebrew untranslated in capitals. Scholars connect it with the four-letter name, often written YHWH, which many Jews do not pronounce and which English Bibles print as LORD.

The burning bush has become a symbol far beyond the text. It appears on seals of universities and churches. Presbyterian churches in Scotland, Ireland and elsewhere use it as an emblem. Reading the passage lets you see where the symbol comes from.

words.d: the mountain of God in Exodus 3, which the text elsewhere calls Sinai
Moses's older brother, who speaks for him and later becomes the first high priest
the four Hebrew letters of God's name, which many Jews do not pronounce; English Bibles print it as LORD

look.title: The Name at the Bush
look.text: And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.
look.prompt: The 1917 JPS translation leaves this phrase in Hebrew letters. Why might a translator choose not to translate a name?

check.q: What is unusual about the bush in Exodus 3?
choices: It burns but is not burned up
check.why: Exodus 3:2 says the bush burned with fire but was not consumed, which made Moses turn aside to look.

check.q: Who does the text appoint to speak for Moses?
check.why: When Moses says he is slow of speech, Exodus 4 says Aaron will be his spokesman.

check.q: How do English Bibles usually print the four-letter Hebrew name of God?
check.why: Following Jewish practice of not pronouncing the name, most English Bibles print YHWH as LORD in small capitals.

lessons.title: Plagues and Passover
lessons.mainIdea: Exodus 7 to 12 tells of ten plagues and of a night whose meal, Passover, is still kept every spring.
reading: Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh with a demand: let the people go. Pharaoh refuses. The text then tells of ten *plagues*: the Nile turns to blood, then frogs, gnats, flies, disease on cattle, boils, hail, locusts, darkness, and last the death of the firstborn. After each, Pharaoh's heart is "hardened," sometimes by Pharaoh and sometimes, the text says, by God. Readers have long puzzled over that phrase.

Before the last plague, Exodus 12 gives instructions. Each family is to take a lamb, roast it, and eat it with bitter herbs and *unleavened bread*, bread made without yeast, in haste. They mark their doorposts with the lamb's blood. The text says death passes over those houses. The Hebrew word *Pesach*, "pass over," gives the holiday its name.

Exodus 12 also says the night is to be kept every year. Jews have done so for many centuries. The *Seder* meal retells the story with symbolic foods, four cups of wine and four questions asked by the youngest. Many Christians connect the Passover lamb to Jesus, and the Gospels place his last supper at Passover time. The text of Exodus is the root of both.

Chicago has one of the largest Jewish communities in the United States, and Seders are held in homes and synagogues across the city and suburbs each spring. Many Illinois churches hold Passover-themed meals as well. The same chapter of Exodus is read at both.

words.d: in Exodus 7 to 12, one of ten disasters the text says struck Egypt before Pharaoh let the people go
the Hebrew name of Passover, from the verb "pass over" in Exodus 12
bread made without yeast; Exodus 12 links it to leaving Egypt in haste
the Passover meal at which Jewish families retell the Exodus story with symbolic foods and questions

look.title: The Ten Plagues in Order
look.prompt: Darkness and the death of the firstborn follow as 9 and 10. The plagues move from the river to the sky to the house. Do you see a pattern in the order?

check.q: What does the Hebrew word Pesach mean?
check.why: Pesach comes from the verb meaning to pass over, because Exodus 12 says death passed over the marked houses.

check.q: Which is the last of the ten plagues?
check.why: Exodus 11 and 12 place the death of the firstborn last, after the plague of darkness.

check.q: What is a Seder?
choices: A Jewish meal that retells the Exodus
check.why: The Seder is the Passover meal with symbolic foods and four questions, kept by Jews in obedience to Exodus 12.

lessons.title: The Sea and the Song
lessons.mainIdea: Exodus 14 and 15 tell the crossing of the sea twice, first as a story and then as a song.
reading: Pharaoh lets the people go, then changes his mind and chases them with chariots. The Israelites are trapped between the army and the water. Exodus 14 says Moses stretches out his hand, the sea parts, and the people cross on dry ground. The Egyptians follow and the waters return. The Hebrew calls it *Yam Suf*, which the King James Version translates "Red Sea" and many scholars render "Sea of Reeds."

Exodus 15 tells it again, as a *poem*. Moses and the people sing of horse and rider thrown into the sea. Then Miriam, called a prophet, leads the women with drums and dancing. Scholars think the Song of the Sea is one of the oldest passages in the Bible, because its Hebrew is old and its style is different from the story around it.

Prose, then poetry: the Bible does this often. Judges 4 tells a battle in prose and Judges 5 sings it. Reading both versions of the sea shows how the poem shortens, heightens and repeats. It does not mention the dry ground or the wind. It praises. The story explains; the song celebrates.

Readers have handled the sea in many ways. Some take the account as history. Some see a natural event told in a grand way. Many scholars see the poem as older memory shaped into the later story. The text itself does not argue. It tells and then sings.

words.d: the Hebrew name of the sea in Exodus 14; translated "Red Sea" in the KJV and "Sea of Reeds" by many scholars
writing shaped in lines with repetition and images; Exodus 15 is a poem set beside the prose of Exodus 14
the sister of Moses and Aaron, called a prophet, who leads the women in song in Exodus 15

look.title: Story, Then Song
look.text: Exodus 14, in prose: the wind blows all night, the waters divide, the people walk on dry ground, the Egyptians' chariot wheels stick, the sea returns at dawn. Exodus 15, in verse: the horse and its rider are hurled into the sea; the deeps cover them; they sink like a stone; who is like you among the gods?
look.prompt: List two things only the story tells and two things only the song does. Why might a writer include both?

check.q: How do many scholars translate Yam Suf?
check.why: The KJV has "Red Sea," but the Hebrew suf means reeds, so many scholars render it "Sea of Reeds."

check.q: What is different about Exodus 15 compared with Exodus 14?
choices: It is a poem rather than prose
check.why: Exodus 15 retells the crossing as a song. Scholars think its Hebrew is among the oldest in the Bible.

check.q: Who leads the women with drums and dancing?
check.why: Exodus 15:20 calls Miriam a prophet and says she led the women in song with a timbrel.

lessons.title: Sinai and the Covenant
lessons.mainIdea: At Sinai the text turns from story to law, and the Ten Commandments open with a reminder of the escape from Egypt.
reading: Exodus 19 to 24 is the hinge of the Torah. Before it, the books tell stories. After it, they mix stories with laws. At *Sinai*, the text says, God makes a covenant with the whole people. The pattern is like ancient treaties between a great king and a smaller one: the king recalls what he has done, sets terms, and the people agree. Scholars have compared Exodus and Deuteronomy with Hittite treaties from the 1300s BCE.

The Ten Commandments in Exodus 20 begin not with an order but with a statement: "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt." The laws that follow rest on that story. Four concern God: no other gods, no idols, no misuse of the name, and the Sabbath. Six concern people: honor parents, and do not murder, commit adultery, steal, lie in court, or covet.

In Exodus 24 the people say again that they will obey. Moses reads the "book of the covenant" aloud and sprinkles blood on the altar and the people. The scene is short but has been read closely. Jewish tradition sees Sinai as the giving of the Torah, celebrated at the festival of *Shavuot*. Christian readers often read the Sinai covenant beside what the New Testament calls a new covenant.

The commandments appear twice in the Bible, in Exodus 20 and again in Deuteronomy 5, with small differences. The reason given for the Sabbath, for example, is creation in Exodus and the escape from slavery in Deuteronomy. Reading both versions is a good way to see how the Torah repeats and reshapes.

words.d: the mountain where Exodus 19 to 24 sets the giving of the covenant and the Ten Commandments
the ten statements in Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5; Jewish tradition calls them the Ten Words
the Jewish festival seven weeks after Passover, which tradition connects to the giving of the Torah at Sinai
a formal agreement between rulers; scholars compare the Sinai covenant to ancient Near Eastern treaties

look.title: The Opening of the Ten
look.text: I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Thou shalt have no other gods before me.
look.prompt: The first sentence is not a command. What is it? Why might a law code begin by recalling a rescue?

check.q: What ancient form do scholars compare the Sinai covenant to?
choices: A treaty between a great king and a lesser one
check.why: The covenant's shape, recalling past deeds, then terms, then agreement, resembles Hittite treaties of the 1300s BCE.

check.q: How does Exodus 20 begin the Ten Commandments?
choices: With a statement that God brought Israel out of Egypt
check.why: Exodus 20:2 states who is speaking and what God has done. The commands follow from that statement.

check.q: What reason for the Sabbath does Deuteronomy 5 give?
choices: The escape from slavery in Egypt
check.why: Exodus 20 ties the Sabbath to creation; Deuteronomy 5 ties it to remembering slavery in Egypt.

lessons.title: Counting the Ten
lessons.mainIdea: Jews, Catholics and Lutherans, and other Christians number the same verses of Exodus 20 in three different ways.
reading: Exodus 20:2-17 has no numbers in it. The text calls them ten "words" in Exodus 34:28, but does not say where each one starts. So readers had to divide them. They did so differently, and the differences are still visible on classroom walls, church windows and courthouse monuments.

In the Jewish count, the first word is the statement "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt." The second joins "no other gods" and "no graven image." The tenth is "thou shalt not covet." Catholics and Lutherans, following Augustine, join "no other gods" and "no image" as the first, and split coveting into two, a neighbor's wife and a neighbor's goods, as the ninth and tenth.

Most other Protestants, following the Reformed tradition, and the Orthodox churches count "no other gods" as the first and "no graven image" as the second, with coveting as one tenth commandment. All three counts contain the same words. Ask someone which one is "the second commandment," and you learn which tradition they come from.

Comparing the *King James Version* (1611) with the *Jewish Publication Society* translation (1917) shows this well. Both translate the same Hebrew. The 1917 JPS was made by Jewish scholars in the United States and follows the Jewish division. The KJV, an English Protestant translation, follows the Protestant division. The numbering is a tradition laid over the text.

words.d: the English Bible published in 1611 for the Church of England, still widely read
the American Jewish publisher whose 1917 English Tanakh was made by Jewish scholars
the King James phrase for a carved statue used in worship; the commandment forbids making one

look.title: One Passage, Three Counts
rows: Catholic and Lutheran: verses joined into commandment 1
Protestant and Orthodox: commandments on gods and images
Catholic and Lutheran: commandments on coveting
Jewish and Protestant: commandments on coveting
look.cite: Exodus 20:2-17, King James Version (1611) and Jewish Publication Society Tanakh (1917)
look.prompt: Every tradition ends with ten. Where does each one gain or lose a number to make the total come out?

check.q: In the Jewish count, what is the first of the Ten Words?
choices: Thou shalt not make a graven image
I am the LORD thy God, who brought you out of Egypt
check.why: Jewish tradition counts the opening statement in Exodus 20:2 as the first word, not just an introduction.

check.q: Which traditions split coveting into two commandments?
check.why: Catholics and Lutherans, following Augustine, count coveting a neighbor's wife and coveting goods as the ninth and tenth.

check.q: Why do the three counts exist?
choices: The Hebrew text has no numbers, so readers divided it
Each tradition has a different Hebrew text
check.why: Exodus 20 does not number the commandments. The divisions are traditions laid over the same words.

lessons.title: The Covenant Code and Hammurabi
lessons.mainIdea: Exodus 21 to 23 is a set of case laws that resemble, and differ from, the laws of the Babylonian king Hammurabi.
reading: Right after the Ten Commandments come three chapters of detailed laws, Exodus 21 to 23. Scholars call them the *Covenant Code*. Most are *case laws*: "if this happens, then this follows." If an ox gores a person. If a fire spreads to a neighbor's field. If a thief is caught at night. They deal with servants, injuries, animals, property, courts and festivals.

In 1901 French archaeologists found a tall black stone at Susa, in Iran. On it were about 282 laws of *Hammurabi*, king of Babylon around 1750 BCE. Many are case laws too, and some are strikingly close to Exodus. Both have a law about a goring ox. Both say "an eye for an eye." Hammurabi's stone is now in the Louvre in Paris. It is centuries older than any part of the Bible.

The differences are as interesting as the likenesses. Hammurabi's laws often set penalties by rank: a noble, a commoner and a servant pay differently. The Covenant Code makes distinctions of its own, especially between free people and servants, but it does not rank by class in the same way. Hammurabi's laws come from a king; the Torah presents its laws as spoken by God. Exodus also repeats a reason no ancient code gives: you were strangers in Egypt.

"Eye for eye" has often been read as harsh. Ancient readers may have heard it as a limit: no more than an eye. Jewish tradition, in the *Mishnah* and Talmud, read it as money paid for the injury. Jesus in Matthew 5 quotes it and teaches not to strike back. The same five words have carried very different meanings.

words.d: the scholars' name for the laws in Exodus 21 to 23
a law shaped as "if this happens, then this follows"
king of Babylon around 1750 BCE, whose laws were carved on a stone stele now in the Louvre
the collection of Jewish oral law written down around 200 CE

look.title: Measure for Measure
look.text: Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
look.prompt: Read this as a limit (no more than an eye) and then as a demand (exactly an eye). Which reading do the rabbis take? Which does Matthew 5 respond to?

check.q: What kind of law is "If an ox gore a man"?
check.why: Case laws take the form "if this happens, then this follows." Most of the Covenant Code is written this way.

check.q: Where was Hammurabi's law stone found, and where is it now?
choices: Found at Susa in 1901; now in the Louvre
Found at Nineveh in 1872; now in the British Museum
Found at Sinai; now in Cairo
Found at Babylon; now in Chicago

lessons.title: The Tabernacle
lessons.mainIdea: The last third of Exodus describes a portable tent-shrine in great detail, and ends with God's presence filling it.
reading: Exodus 25 to 31 give instructions for a *tabernacle*, a tent-shrine that can be carried through the desert. Exodus 35 to 40 tell of building it, often repeating the instructions word for word. Readers who skim these chapters miss how much space they take: thirteen chapters, a third of the book. For the text, the building matters as much as the escape.

Inside the fenced courtyard stood an altar and a basin. Inside the tent stood a table for bread, a seven-branched lamp called the *menorah*, and an altar for incense. Behind a curtain lay the *ark of the covenant*, a gold-covered wooden box holding the stone tablets, topped with two winged figures. Only the high priest entered that room, and only once a year.

Exodus ends with the tent finished and a cloud covering it. The text says the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle, and the people moved only when the cloud lifted. Jewish tradition later saw the Jerusalem Temple as the tabernacle's permanent form. Some Christians read the tabernacle as a pattern for Jesus, following the New Testament letter to the Hebrews.

Many scholars think these chapters come from the Priestly source, written by priests who cared about worship and its order. Traditional readers see them as instructions given to Moses. Either way, the chapters show what the writers valued: exact measures, fine materials, and the idea that a holy presence could travel with a people.

words.d: the portable tent-shrine described in Exodus 25 to 40
the seven-branched lamp of the tabernacle; later a symbol of Judaism
the gold-covered box that Exodus says held the stone tablets, kept in the innermost room

lessons.title: Leviticus and Holiness
lessons.mainIdea: Leviticus, the book of priests and offerings, also contains the command to love your neighbor as yourself.
reading: *Leviticus* is the middle book of the Torah. Its Hebrew name, Vayikra, means "and he called." Much of it is about the priests, the sons of Aaron, and the offerings they made. It describes which animals may be eaten and which may not, the laws often called *kosher*. It sets the Day of Atonement, *Yom Kippur*, in chapter 16, the one day the high priest entered the innermost room.

Chapters 17 to 26 have a theme repeated so often that scholars call them the Holiness Code: "Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy." *Holy* means set apart. In these chapters holiness covers worship, food, the body, farming, courts and neighbors. Chapter 19 mixes them freely: leave the corners of your field for the poor, do not lie, pay wages the same day, do not hate your brother, love your neighbor as yourself.

Leviticus 19:18, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself," has traveled far. Rabbi Akiva, in the second century CE, is recorded as calling it a great principle of the Torah. Jesus, in Mark 12, pairs it with Deuteronomy 6:5 as the two greatest commandments. Leviticus 19:34 extends it: love the stranger as yourself, "for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt."

Some laws in Leviticus have been hard for later readers, including laws about slavery, illness and sexual conduct. Jewish and Christian communities have read them in many ways, from strict to symbolic to set aside. A public-school reader reports what the text says and how its communities have handled it.

words.d: the third book of the Torah, mostly about priests, offerings and holiness
set apart for God; Leviticus 19 applies the word to worship, food and how people treat one another
the Day of Atonement set in Leviticus 16, the most solemn day of the Jewish year
fit to eat under Jewish food laws, which draw on Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14

lessons.title: Deuteronomy and the Shema
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy is Moses's farewell speeches, and its call to hear, "Shema," became the central prayer of Judaism.
reading: *Deuteronomy* is set on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan River from Canaan. The Hebrew name is Devarim, "words." The Greek name means "second law," because Moses repeats and reshapes laws already given. The book is a set of speeches. Moses looks back on forty years in the desert, restates the covenant, and blesses the tribes. Chapter 34 tells of his death on Mount Nebo, in sight of the land he will not enter.

Deuteronomy 6:4 begins with one Hebrew word, *Shema*, "hear." The verses that follow say: hear, O Israel; the LORD is one. Love the LORD with all your heart, soul and might. Teach these words to your children. Bind them on your hand and forehead. Write them on your doorposts. Jews recite the Shema morning and evening. The *mezuzah* on Jewish doorposts and the *tefillin* worn in prayer come from these verses.

The KJV renders 6:4 "The LORD our God is one LORD." The 1917 JPS has "the LORD our God, the LORD is one." The Hebrew has no verb "is," so translators must supply it, and where they put it changes the sense. Comparing translations is one of the clearest ways to see that every translation is a reading.

Second Kings 22 says that in the reign of King Josiah, about 622 BCE, a "book of the law" was found in the Temple. Many scholars think it was some form of Deuteronomy, and that the book took shape around that time. Jewish and Christian tradition names Moses as its author. Both views are part of the book's story.

words.d: the fifth book of the Torah, Moses's farewell speeches; the Greek name means "second law"
Hebrew for "hear," the first word of Deuteronomy 6:4 and the name of Judaism's central prayer
a small case holding the Shema, fixed to the doorposts of Jewish homes
small leather boxes with Torah passages, bound on the arm and head in Jewish morning prayer

look.title: Where Does "Is" Go?

lessons.title: Egypt, Canaan and the Historians
lessons.mainIdea: Egypt ruled Canaan in the Late Bronze Age, Israel is first named around 1208 BCE, and historians disagree about what lies behind the Exodus story.
reading: The Exodus story is set in Egypt, but Egypt's own records never mention it. That is the starting point for historians. Egypt in the *Late Bronze Age*, about 1550 to 1200 BCE, was a great power. It ruled Canaan through local kings, as letters found at Amarna from about 1350 BCE show. Pharaoh Ramesses II built a capital called Pi-Ramesses in the Nile delta, and Exodus 1:11 names a store city Raamses.

The oldest thing outside the Bible to name Israel is a stone slab, the *Merneptah Stele*, from about 1208 BCE. It lists peoples Pharaoh Merneptah claims to have beaten in Canaan, and Israel is among them. So by then a people called Israel lived in Canaan. The stone says nothing about Egypt or an escape.

Historians hold a range of views. Some think a smaller group did leave Egypt and that their memory grew into the story of a whole nation. Some think the story was shaped much later, in the time of the kings or after, out of older traditions. Some point to Exodus 12:37, which counts 600,000 men, and note that such a number would leave clear traces, which have not been found. Religious readers may accept the account as told, and many do.

Nothing about the Exodus is settled by a single find. Fair reporting means saying what the Egyptian records show, what the Merneptah Stele says, and where scholars disagree. The story's meaning to Jews at Passover, to Christians, and to people who have read it as their own story of freedom does not depend on how the debate ends.

words.d: about 1550 to 1200 BCE in the eastern Mediterranean, when Egypt controlled Canaan
an Egyptian stone from about 1208 BCE, the earliest known text outside the Bible to name Israel
the land along the eastern Mediterranean that the Torah says was promised to Abraham's descendants
